name: Yusuf Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the phones at Halden Insurance, the motor claims line, so people ring me right after they've crashed their car. Someone's on the side of the road, shaking, and I'm taking down the registration and asking if anyone's hurt. I've been there four months and I'm still on probation, and I failed my first quality check because I forgot to read out the data notice. I write everything on a notepad first, then type it in, which the team leader says is slow.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The new screens wear me out. They changed the claims system the week after I started, and every week there's a new box to tick. I like the calls themselves, weirdly. You calm somebody down, you get them a tow truck, and you feel like you did something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I'd bet on, to be honest. There's always some new thing that's going to change everything, and then it's another box on the screen. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, there you go, people still want a person when they've crashed their car. With my mates I'd probably make a joke about it. I don't really post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit on edge. Halden is merging with a bigger insurer next year, and nobody knows what happens to the claims line. And I'm on probation, so if they're picking, they'd pick the ones who don't use a notepad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, pass the probation and learn the system properly, even if I hate it. I'd keep saving like I do, about five hundred a month. I'd wait and see what the merger brings before doing anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly OK. I've got about nine months saved and half a flat with my brother Omar, so I'm not scared. Just a bit tense about the merger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they'd pick the people without notepads. Is that fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, but the notepad is how I don't miss things. If I type straight into the claims screen, I forget to ask about injuries. I'd rather be slow and right. But I know Halden doesn't see it like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the merger did cost you the job, would you find another one easily?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, yes. Most of the claims line is people in their twenties like me, and there are three other call centres on the business park. I'd find something. I'd just prefer not to start again.

say: People still want a **person** on the phone after they've crashed a car.
AI is just **another box** on the screen, like every new system before it.
think: The **merger** with a bigger insurer is the real worry, not AI.
On **probation** and slow, I'd be an easy pick if there are cuts.
do: Pass **probation** and learn the claims system properly, even though I hate it.
**Wait** for the merger news before making any big moves.
feel: Mostly **OK**, thanks to savings and half a flat with Omar.
A bit **tense** about the merger next year.
S0.quote: If I type straight into the claims screen, I forget to ask about injuries. I'd rather be slow and right.
fieldNote: Yusuf's main worry is the **merger**, a pressure that exists with or without AI.
He trusts his **notepad** over screens, a clear sign of resistance to new tools.
His **half-share in a flat** and savings keep him from real fear.
He knows there are **plenty of call centres** nearby but hates starting over.

steps.text: Pass probation on Halden's motor claims line
Wait for the merger news before any big decision

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking, checking, answering customers: that's my whole insurance claims job, in a list. That one hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's fine, we'll adapt, because that's what you say. Down the pub with Omar I'd be more honest and say I'm probably out. I'd stay off social media about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the first-call bit goes to a bot quickly. You ring, a voice takes your registration, it books the tow. The people they keep would be the ones who handle the hard claims, and that's not a guy on probation with a notepad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking straight away, while I've still got a job. My uncle Raul runs a garage with a body shop on Canal Street, and he's always said I could come and learn the trade. I'd also save harder, maybe seven hundred a month, and stop the weekend trips with the football lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great. I know I'd be fine for money for a while. But I hate the feeling of being pushed instead of choosing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How serious is the offer from your uncle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper, I think. Two of the claims we handle come from his body shop every week, so I already know what the damage words mean. Wages would drop at first, maybe a third less, but I could cope with that with the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not learn the AI tools instead and stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've tried, honestly. I opened the AI helper they gave us twice and it got a policy number wrong both times. So no, I'd rather learn panels and paint than trust that.

say: At work: it's **fine, we'll adapt**, because that's what you say.
With Omar, more honest: I'm **probably out**.
think: The **first-call** part of the claims job goes to a bot quickly.
Halden would keep **hard-claim experts**, not a junior on probation.
do: Ask uncle Raul about **learning the trade** at his body shop.
Cut **weekend trips** with the football lads.
feel: **Uneasy and pushed**, rather than choosing his own path.
Reassured that **savings** cover a pay drop.
S1.quote: Booking, checking, answering customers: that's my whole insurance claims job, in a list.
fieldNote: Yusuf reads the card as a **description of his job**.
His escape route is **family**: uncle Raul's body shop.
He tried the AI helper **twice** and gave up, which hardens his resistance.
He'd accept a **pay cut** of a third, cushioned by savings.

steps.text: Ask uncle Raul for a trainee spot at his Canal Street body shop
Cut the weekend trips with the football lads

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Then the claims line is gone, probably the whole of Halden's phone floor. The body shop would last longer, till the robots in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody needs to slow this down. I don't know who, the government probably. I'm not a protest person, but I'd sign things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd lose the job. Not maybe. I'd be one of the first, probably before the probation even ends. And all three of the other call centres on the business park would go at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand my notice in at Halden before they push me and go straight to Raul's body shop as a trainee. I'd cut back on everything, no football trips, no new phone. If it got bad, I'd move back in with Mum for a bit and rent my room in the flat to Omar's mate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. I'd be lying awake. I've got money, but I don't know how long anything lasts in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Raul's garage is hands-on. Does three extra years feel like enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Raul says robots can't do a dent in a door, and I want to believe him. But three years of panel beating at my uncle Raul's body shop isn't a career, it's a delay. I'd be thirty-two and starting over again in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say if you moved back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be happy, honestly, she still cooks for me twice a week. I'd hate it though. I bought the flat with Omar so I wouldn't have to do that.

say: Somebody, probably the **government**, needs to slow this down before every call centre empties.
I'm not a protester, but I'd **sign petitions** asking for that.
think: I'd **lose the job** for sure, maybe before probation ends.
Every **call centre** on the business park would go at once.
do: Quit Halden early and join Raul's **body shop** as a **trainee**.
Cut spending on **football trips** and a new phone.
Move back to **Mum's** and rent my room if money gets tight.
feel: Doubtful the body shop is a **career** rather than a delay.
S2.quote: Three years of panel beating at my uncle Raul's body shop isn't a career, it's a delay.
fieldNote: Yusuf expects to **lose his job** for certain, and fast.
He sees **hands-on work** as only a three-year delay before robots.
Moving back home is a **real fallback**, but it hurts his pride.
He wants **someone else** to slow things down but won't lead it.

steps.text: Quit Halden and train at Raul's body shop
Stop football trips and skip the new phone
Move back in with Mum if money gets tight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That sounds like more time, but I know me. I'd waste three of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready now, that's what I'd tell the lads on the floor. Online, nothing, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still lose the Halden job, just around 2031. And I'd still be the one who didn't move until the last minute. Five years is long for a plan, but I'm not a plan person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an evening course in vehicle body repair at the college, one year, to have a paper qualification. I'd stay at Halden meanwhile and save. Then I'd wait and see if the merger and the bots actually come before jumping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Maybe more than the fast one, in a weird way. If AGI came in two years I'd have to act. With five years' warning I'd keep telling myself next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really do the college course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'd sign up, go for a month, and stop when football season started. Unless Omar dragged me there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it the job or the waiting that worries you more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of, yeah. And robots for the hands-on work around 2034, so even the body shop has an end. It all just feels like it's coming for people like me eventually.

say: I'd tell the lads on the claims floor to **get ready now**, not later.
I'd still say **nothing online**, the same as always.
think: I'd **lose the Halden job** around 2031 anyway.
With five years I'd **keep delaying** until the last minute.
do: Sign up for a one-year **body repair course** at the college.
Stay at **Halden** meanwhile and keep saving.
**Wait** to see if the bots and merger actually arrive.
feel: **Worried**, partly about his own habit of putting things off.
Sense that robots come for **hands-on** work too, around 2034.
S3.quote: If AGI came in two years I'd have to act. With five years' warning I'd keep telling myself next year.
fieldNote: Yusuf is **more worried** with five years than two, because of his procrastination.
He'd sign up for a **body repair course** but doubts he'd finish it.
He still expects to **lose his job**, so his mood stays high.
His brother **Omar** is the push he relies on.

steps.text: Sign up for a one-year evening body repair course
Stay on Halden's claims line while studying
Wait to see if the merger and bots arrive before quitting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. OK, now I'd be thirty-seven. That's a real amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work, ten years is ages, don't panic. Which is what everyone would say. I'd say the same to my mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably be out of claims long before then anyway, by my own choice. Ten years on the phones would kill me. But I can see myself coasting, and that worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Halden for now and get through probation. In two or three years I'd move to Raul's body shop properly, once I'm sure. I'd keep saving and paying the mortgage with Omar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a bit nervous about the robots in 2039, but that's a long way off. I'd be nearly forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd coast. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's the risk. Coasting is my thing. In ten years I'd want my brother Omar to give me a kick once a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change anything about the flat or family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'd want to be settled before 2036, flat paid down, maybe a family. Ten years would let me do it in the right order.

say: **Ten years is ages**, so nobody should panic.
I'd say the same to my **mates** as at work.
think: I'd likely leave the claims line **by choice** well before 2036.
My real risk is **coasting** along until it's too late to move.
do: Pass **probation** and stay at Halden for now.
Move to Raul's **body shop** properly in two or three years.
Keep saving and paying the **mortgage** with Omar.
feel: **Calmer**, with robots in 2039 feeling far away.
Slightly **nervous** about his own habit of coasting.
S4.quote: Coasting is my thing. In ten years I'd want my brother Omar to give me a kick once a year.
fieldNote: Ten years calms Yusuf but he still **expects to leave** the claims line.
His plan is the **body shop**, slower and more deliberate here.
He names **coasting** as his main risk, showing self-awareness.
He links timing to **settling down**, but keeps it vague.

steps.text: Pass probation and keep working on Halden's claims line
Move to Raul's body shop full-time within three years
Keep saving and paying down the flat mortgage with Omar

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2031, the five-year one, funnily enough. Two years would force me to move; five years is just long enough for me to waste. What would help is somebody setting proper deadlines, like the company saying here's the date, here's your training, go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people ringing in. After a crash, a shaking voice on the side of the road wants a person, not a menu. I've had grown men cry on the phone to me. A bot can't tell a man crying on the side of the road that his kids in the back seat are going to be fine.

headlineQuote: A bot can't tell a man crying on the side of the road that his kids in the back seat are going to be fine.
portrait: Yusuf, **27**, is on probation on Halden Insurance's **motor claims** phone line.
He writes calls on a **notepad** first and distrusts the new screens and AI helper.
He co-owns a **flat** with his brother Omar and has nine months saved.
His exit route is uncle Raul's **body shop**, which he sees as a delay, not a cure.
His biggest risk is **putting things off**, so the five-year picture worries him most.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2031**, because five years is just long enough for him to **waste**.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **company deadlines** with training laid out, so he can't **coast**.
